## Mechanism
The tracked chain is supply-then-demand. A higher stocks-to-use ratio loosens the balance sheet and pressures price (high confidence); the harvest-side inputs into that are US yield and acreage, and then, one to three quarters out, the South American crop. The El Nino channel (medium confidence) works by lifting Argentine and southern-Brazil rainfall, raising yields and adding exportable supply — price-pressuring at a one-to-two-quarter lag, which is exactly the window the question asks about. Against it, wide crush margins are a high-confidence price-supportive driver: processors bid aggressively for beans when the board crush is wide, pulling cash demand forward. Managed-money length (medium confidence) amplifies moves in whichever direction the balance sheet breaks, and extreme length also flags reversal risk — it is an amplifier, not a direction.

Where this turns convex: with a large crop and a rebuilt carryout, a normal weather scare is roughly linear — the buffer absorbs it. The convexity would return only if the South American season disappoints into an already-drawn US export program.

## Mechanism
Stocks-to-grindings is the buffer between a supply shock and the price. When it is deep, a lost pod crop is absorbed by carry-out and price moves roughly in line with the shortfall; when it is thin, the same shortfall must be rationed by price, and the response turns convex — the right tail gets fat. Thin certified and end-of-season stocks are also what lets a collapse in deliverable exchange stocks steepen backwardation and spike the front month; that channel and slow port arrivals are the model's highest-confidence real-time tells for a West African deficit. The same low buffer makes the skew asymmetric on the other side: a good crop rebuilds stocks and pressures price, but off a 10th-percentile base it takes more than one benign season to restore a mid-1990s-style cushion.

## The record
- 2023/24: end-of-season stocks fell 28% to 1.270 million tonnes, stocks-to-grindings 26.4% [E1]; grindings that season estimated at 4.81 million tonnes.
- 2024/25: stocks-to-grindings 29.2% [E7]; observed end stocks 1,320 thousand tonnes [N2] against grindings of 4,628 thousand tonnes [N3], ratio 0.28522 [N1].
- Standing: 10th percentile [N4], -1.65671 sigma [N5], against an own-history range of 0.263595 [N6] to 0.475389 [N7].
- The last time the record shows a comfortable market: about 45% at the end of 1995/96 [E2] — a far deeper cushion than today's.

## Mechanism

**The buffer sets the convexity.** The model's core fundamental is the stocks-to-use ratio: a tightening ratio lifts price, a loose one pressures it (high confidence). At 0.273095 [N7] the US carries a real cushion, so an incremental yield or acreage loss is absorbed rather than amplified -- the price response to a domestic supply miss is roughly linear here, not convex. Note also that domestic-use for 2026/27 is not yet published in this record, so the use side of that ratio is only partly visible.

**Where the right tail actually lives.** Two channels can tip nonlinearly:
- *Export policy abroad.* India banning or curtailing non-basmati exports removes a very large share of world trade overnight and spikes CBOT-linked prices (high confidence); minimum export prices and export taxes stack on top, and the model says a squeeze needs several of these to line up at once with strong state tender buying. That is a threshold regime, not a gradient.
- *Weather into Asia.* El Nino suppresses monsoon rainfall over India, Thailand, Indonesia and the Philippines (high confidence), which is precisely what triggers the protective curbs above. The ocean signal is at a strong warm anomaly of 1.8 degC [N20], rising by +0.41 degC over the prior month [N22] and higher in each of the last five months [N23]. The model's lag on this channel is one to three quarters, so the crop consequence sits ahead of us, not behind.

**A US-specific detonator.** A drop in deliverable long-grain stocks against contract specs can make the thin rough rice contract squeeze and detach from cash (medium confidence). That is the one place where the domestic sheet, comfortable as it looks in aggregate, can still go convex -- deliverable supply is not the same as total supply.

**Left tail.** The mirror regime is a supply glut: reserve releases into ample stocks plus a firm dollar and weak exporter currencies let Asian origins undercut, which pressures price. Indian public stocks were revised up as of the December 2025 WASDE [E38], which sits on that side of the ledger.

## The record

- Supply, 2026/27, as published 2026-09-11: production 158.2 million hundredweight [N1], beginning stocks 58.4 million hundredweight [N5], imports 49.8 million hundredweight [N11]; exports 78 million hundredweight [N3]; ending stocks 40.4 million hundredweight [N2]; season-average farm price 14.9 $/cwt [N6]. US harvested area is 0.832 M ha [N17]. Total domestic use for 2026/27 carries no figure in this record -- not yet published -- so I assert nothing for it.
- Crop state: 73 pct of acreage harvested as of 2026-09-22 [N9]; condition last served at 73 pct good-to-excellent on the 2026-09-08 read [N12]. No crop-condition series is available for the broader scope requested -- a coverage gap, not a zero.
- Export flow: weekly exports 151.382 thousand MT [N13], gross new sales 156.93 thousand MT [N14], outstanding sales 139.176 thousand MT [N15].
- Stocks abroad: 2025/26 global rice beginning stocks were raised, primarily for India, on higher-than-expected Food Corporation of India stocks [E38].
- Precedent for the price response when the sheet moves: the settled USDA season-average farm price rose from $10.40/cwt [N25] in 2016/17 to $12.90/cwt [N26] in 2017/18 -- a survey-based actual, not a futures settle. The 2017/18 tightening had an identified cause in the record: the 2017/18 production cut was all on a large reduction in long-grain acreage per the March 31 Prospective Plantings survey [E9]. That is the shape of the acreage-to-price channel, dated to 2017.
- Cost floor: Brent crude sits at a 5-year z-score of 0.507294 [N21], up +0.5124 over the prior month [N24]. The model's crude-to-rice cost channel is low confidence -- treat it as a hypothesis about the production cost floor, not an established driver.

## Where the record disagrees

The two ocean-state drivers point opposite ways and the model does not rank them identically. El Nino is the high-confidence channel: it suppresses the Asian monsoon, cuts production and triggers export curbs -- price-supportive. La Nina is medium confidence and its documented consequences cut both ways: a 2025 outlook warned La Nina could cause flooding or landslides across East and South Asia, disrupting rice planting [E31], while an earlier assessment tied severe drought losses in Rio Grande do Sul irrigated rice to La Nina [E30]. Given the current warm anomaly [N20] and the higher confidence tag, the El Nino leg is the one to weight -- and that is a model ranking, not a measured historical attribution.

## What to watch

- **Indian export policy** -- any move on non-basmati restrictions, a minimum export price, or a parboiled levy. This is the single highest-confidence lever in the model and it works within zero to one quarter.
- **The ocean anomaly trend** [N20][N22][N23] and then, one to three quarters later, the Indian kharif monsoon. The 2014/15 precedent in the record: global production was cut on slower kharif planting from a late monsoon start [E22].
- **Deliverable long-grain stocks against contract specs** -- the thin-contract squeeze channel is the only domestic route to a convex move while the stocks-to-use buffer [N7] holds.
- **Buyer tenders** from the Philippines and Indonesia; note Indonesia's 2026 Commodity Balance significantly reduced 2025/26 rice and corn import quotas [E26], which works against the tender-demand leg.
- **The dollar and exporter currencies** -- the loosening side. The record shows a strong dollar facilitating Brazilian rice exports as of October 2015 [E16], the undercut mechanism in action.

One honesty note: the newest dated document here is 2026-04-01 and the number rows are read as of 2026-09-26, so the balance-sheet picture is current while the policy narrative rests on older documents. A live read on what India is doing today is not available in this record.

On the "this year" part I have to correct the framing: the record here shows the US export program is not visibly collapsing -- weekly export sales rose in each of the last three weeks [N4] and the latest weekly change was +164.219 1000 MT [N3], while Brazil's MY2026 exports stand at 118 MMT [N2]; a full current-season US balance sheet is not in this evidence.
raw_draft.postverify_mechanism:
## Mechanism
**The tariff channel is a demand-reroute, not a supply shock.** A Chinese duty on US-origin beans makes Brazilian origin cheaper into China at the same world price, so Chinese crushers shift purchases south. Three consequences follow in the model, all high-confidence: the US export sales pace slows, a slow pace signals weak demand and builds US ending stocks, and a higher stocks-to-use ratio loosens the balance sheet and points toward lower CBOT prices. Brazilian FOB premiums firm at the same time -- the pressure is specific to the US-Gulf-linked benchmark, not to the world bean. Two drivers firing together (tariff plus lagging export pace) are what the model calls a tariff-driven reroute regime; near this as-of no soybean regime has enough drivers documented to say the conditions line up.

Where it turns convex: the tariff itself is roughly linear on the flat price, but the balance-sheet leg is not -- once carryout is already ample, further export loss compounds into the stocks-to-use ratio and the price response steepens to the downside. Conversely, a tariff *removal* is asymmetric the other way only if the crop is tight.

## The record
Dated sequence, by event date:
- 2018-03: after China imposed 25 percent tariffs, soybean prices dropped significantly [E1]; the additional 25 percent on top of the normal 3 percent duty took effect 2018-07-06 [E2], and WASDE flagged the duties as affecting 2018/19 US soybean and product trade on 2018-07-12 [E3]. The price response was documented within the same season as the measure -- fast relative to the driver's stated zero-to-two-quarter lag.
- 2018-09: in the corn record, the same tariffs raised corn and corn-product inclusion in feed rations as a partial substitute for rising soymeal protein prices [E9] -- the shock did not stay inside beans.
- 2020-03-02: China's tariff exclusion process for the Section 301 retaliatory duties, after which US soybean exports to China recovered in MY 2020/21 -- roughly a marketing year for the flow to come back, slower than the price fell.
- 2025-03-04: a 10 percent tariff on US soybeans, with GAIN reporting retaliatory duties in place as of 2025-03-19 [E5][E7]; 2025-10-30: the Busan deal eased tariff pressures.
- Balance-sheet context, reported 2025-05-12: the US share of global soybean exports was forecast at 26 percent in 2025/26, down from 28 percent in 2024/25, despite higher global demand [E47] -- share loss is the durable footprint the model predicts.

Observed now (as of 2026-09-26): weekly exports rose in each of the last 3 weeks [N4], the latest weekly change was +164.219 1000 MT [N3], and Brazil's MY2026 exports are 118 MMT [N2]. One weekly row prints 0 1000 MT for 2025-09-26..2026-09-26 [N1] -- read it as what it is, a single series row, not a season verdict.

Also in the record, a third-order coincidence walk on the October-to-December 2021 window that low-water-on-the-Mississippi defines -- it is not a tariff window, so treat it as how the complex co-moves, not as tariff evidence. CBOT soybeans changed +3.0297 % [N5] and CBOT soybean meal +20.3115 % [N9]; the declared crush relation between soybeans and soybean meal held on this firing, in-sample on that window only. CBOT soybean oil changed -13.8627 % [N10] and the declared relation between meal and oil held on this firing. CME palm oil changed -9.2896 % [N11] and the declared relation between soybean oil and palm oil held on this firing. On the boards settling in different currencies, ZCE rapeseed meal changed +10.2056 % [N6] and ZCE rapeseed oil +3.8779 % [N8] -- each a move inside Chinese yuan against CBOT soybeans' move inside US dollars, with the declared relation holding on each firing, read on each board's own-currency move, so the exchange-rate move sits inside that comparison and is not removed from it; the Chinese yuan per US dollar rate changed -1.1012 % over 2021-10-08 through 2021-12-20 [N7]. MATIF rapeseed cannot be read on this window: it predates that board's own price history. Every one of these windows ended 2021-12-20, four years before this as-of -- dated history, not a current read.

## Where the record disagrees
The trade-policy record does not run one way. The 2018 leg is unambiguous price pressure on US beans [E1][E3]. But the 2020 exclusion process shows the channel reverses -- US exports to China recovered in MY 2020/21 -- and the 2025 leg was eased at Busan, while the corn record notes that after China cut its additional corn tariff to 10 percent as of 2025-11-10, US corn purchases had still not resumed as of March 2026 [E10][E11]. That is the honest asymmetry: tariffs cut the flow faster than their removal restores it, and a headline reduction is not a purchase.

## What to watch
- Weekly US export sales pace and commitments against the Chinese share -- the fastest-reading confirmation that the reroute is or is not biting.
- The US stocks-to-use ratio in successive WASDE prints; that is where a slow pace converts into a loose balance sheet and where the downside steepens.
- Whether the eased tariff setting actually converts to booked Chinese business in US origin, given the corn precedent [E10].
- Brazilian exportable supply and the CONAB production track -- the size of the alternative origin sets how much demand the reroute can absorb.

The model's highest-confidence loosening channel is the stocks-to-use ratio: a higher ratio signals a looser sheet and pressures price. A large crop plus a rebuilt carryout is exactly that configuration, and it caps the upside from any single friendly headline — a big number is not repriced upward until the buffer thins.

The two channels that could have turned it higher over the following quarter:
- **South American supply** — downward CONAB revisions to Brazil tighten global supply expectations (high confidence); February's WASDE already flagged lower Brazilian yield on adverse weather in southern Mato Grosso and Parana [E25], offsetting higher harvested area.

Against those, a strong dollar pressures dollar-denominated prices [E35] and positioning was a headwind, not a tailwind.

The record carries no figure for US total domestic use or for world ending stocks/production in 2023/24 at this as-of — not yet published, so no level can be asserted.
